topics.title: Girls' education: formal letter of complaint

learn.hook: A girl everyone called 'simpleton' ends the story by speaking up louder than anyone. What changed her?
points: 'Bholi' by K.A. Abbas is about Sulekha, nicknamed Bholi, a girl who was laughed at and ignored at home.
She is sent to school, where a kind teacher encourages her. Education gives her knowledge, courage and self-respect.
In India, the Right to Education Act, 2009, gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14.
A letter of complaint is a formal letter: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, Sir/Madam, body, Yours faithfully, name.
Body of a complaint: state the problem, give exact details (where, since when, effects), request specific action, and thank the reader.

example.q: Passage: When Lata joined the village school at nine, she hid behind the last bench. Her teacher, Sunita Ma'am, lent her a picture book every Friday. A year later, Lata read the Republic Day speech aloud to the whole school. What changed Lata, and what does this show about education?
steps: At first she hid behind the last bench: she was shy.
Her teacher kept lending her books: encouragement.
A year later she spoke to the whole school: education and a caring teacher built her confidence.
example.answer: Her teacher's encouragement and books; education builds a child's confidence.

learn.reallife: Schemes like 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' (launched in 2015) encourage families to educate their daughters.

games.title: Bholi and letters
items: Bholi's teacher makes fun of her stammer.
Her teacher is kind and encourages her.

quiz.explain: 'Bholi' is a nickname; her real name is Sulekha.
steps: 'Bholi' (simpleton) is only a nickname.
Her real name is Sulekha.
Answer: Sulekha
quiz.mistake: Takes the nickname as her real name

quiz.explain: Her kind teacher encourages her to speak and learn.
steps: At school, a kind teacher encourages Bholi to speak and learn.
Her teacher helps her gain confidence.
Answer: Her teacher

quiz.q: Why does Bholi refuse to marry Bishamber at the end?
options: She wants to move to the city
He demands a dowry, showing his greed, and she now has self-respect
Her teacher tells her to refuse
quiz.explain: Education gave her the courage to reject a greedy man.
steps: Bishamber demands a dowry at the wedding.
Educated and self-respecting now, Bholi refuses to marry such a greedy man.
Answer: He demands a dowry, showing his greed, and she now has self-respect
quiz.mistake: Credits someone else with her decision

quiz.q: The Right to Education Act, 2009, gives free and compulsory education to children of which age group?
quiz.explain: The Act covers children from 6 to 14 years.
steps: The Right to Education Act, 2009, makes education free and compulsory.
It covers children aged 6 to 14 years.
Answer: 6 to 14 years

quiz.q: Passage: When Lata joined the village school at nine, she hid behind the last bench. Her teacher, Sunita Ma'am, lent her a picture book every Friday. A year later, Lata read the Republic Day speech aloud to the whole school. What helped Lata change?
options: Moving to the front bench by force
Winning a prize on her first day
quiz.explain: Sunita Ma'am lent her a picture book every Friday.
steps: Sunita Ma'am lent Lata a picture book every Friday.
Her teacher's encouragement and books helped Lata change.
Answer: Her teacher's encouragement and books
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail not in the passage

quiz.q: What should the body of a letter of complaint include?
options: The problem, its details and the action requested
A long story about your holidays
quiz.explain: A complaint must say what is wrong and what you want done.
steps: A complaint must state what is wrong and what should be done.
So the body includes the problem, its details and the action requested.
Answer: The problem, its details and the action requested

quiz.q: Which is the best subject line for a complaint letter?
options: Subject: Broken streetlights on the road to the girls' school
quiz.explain: It is short, specific and states the issue.
steps: A good subject line is short and specific.
'Broken streetlights on the road to the girls' school' names the exact issue.
Answer: Subject: Broken streetlights on the road to the girls' school

quiz.explain: il- (not) + literate (able to read and write).
steps: il- means not; literate means able to read and write.
So illiterate means unable to read and write.
Answer: Unable to read and write
quiz.mistake: Does not know the prefix il- means not

teach.ask: Gappu: Why did going to school change Bholi so much? And how would I complain about a broken school gate?
teach.praise: Brave-chirp! Education gave Bholi confidence, and a formal letter with a clear subject gets problems fixed!
teach.nudge: What did school give Bholi? And what kind of letter would you write about a problem?

revise.summary: In K.A. Abbas's 'Bholi', Sulekha, laughed at and ignored at home, is encouraged by a kind teacher, and education gives her knowledge, courage and self-respect. We also learn the formal letter of complaint.
focus: Recall Bholi's real name, who helped her and why she refuses Bishamber.
Know what the Right to Education Act, 2009, provides.
Write a complaint letter with problem, details and requested action.
remember: The Right to Education Act, 2009, gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14.
Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, Sir/Madam, body, Yours faithfully, name.
Body: state the problem, give exact details (where, since when, effects), request specific action, thank the reader.
traps: 'Bholi' is a nickname; her real name is Sulekha.
Don't just complain; a complaint letter must request specific action.
Don't write a vague subject line; keep it short and specific.

topics.title: Self-confidence: modals of ability, permission and duty

learn.hook: 'I can.' 'I may.' 'I must.' Tiny words, but they say a lot about confidence!
points: As a child, Bholi stammered and was mocked, so she hardly spoke.
At school she learns to speak and read. At the end she speaks firmly and decides to teach at the school where she learnt so much.
Modals show ability (can, could), permission (may, can), obligation (must, have to), advice (should) and no necessity (needn't).
'Must' shows strong obligation, often from the speaker; 'have to' often shows a rule from outside: 'We have to wear uniforms.'
'Could' is the past of 'can' for ability: 'At five, I could swim.'

example.q: Choose modals: 'At first Bholi ___ not speak clearly. Later she ___ speak confidently. Everyone ___ respect her choice.'
steps: First blank: past inability: could.
Second: ability she gained: could (or was able to).
Third: a strong duty: must.

learn.reallife: Confident speakers say 'I can try' instead of 'I can't'. School debates and assemblies build this skill.

items.text: You ___ wear a helmet on a scooter; it's the law.
When I was five, I ___ swim.
You ___ bring lunch; it will be served at the camp.
You look tired. You ___ rest for a while.

quiz.q: What difficulty did Bholi have as a child?
quiz.explain: Her stammer made her shy and the target of teasing.
steps: Bholi was shy because of how she spoke.
She stammered, and others teased her.
Answer: She stammered when she spoke

quiz.q: What does Bholi decide to do at the end?
options: Teach at the school where she studied
quiz.explain: She will care for her parents and teach at her school.
steps: At the end, Bholi chooses to look after her parents.
She will teach at the school where she studied.
Answer: Teach at the school where she studied

quiz.q: Choose the modal: 'You ___ wear a seat belt; it is the law.'
quiz.explain: A legal rule is a strong obligation: must.
steps: Wearing a seat belt is the law — a strong obligation.
Strong obligation takes 'must'.
Answer: must

quiz.q: Choose the modal: '___ I borrow your pen, please?'
steps: The speaker is politely asking permission.
Polite permission is asked with 'May'.
Answer: May
quiz.mistake: Uses a modal of obligation for a request

quiz.q: Choose the modal: 'She ___ speak three languages fluently.'
steps: Speaking three languages is an ability.
Ability takes 'can'.
Answer: can

quiz.q: Choose the modal: 'You ___ bring lunch; it will be served.'
steps: Lunch will be served, so bringing it is not necessary.
Lack of necessity is shown by 'needn't'.
Answer: needn't

quiz.q: Choose the modal: 'When I was six, I ___ ride a bicycle.'
quiz.explain: 'Could' is the past form of 'can' for ability.
steps: 'When I was six' shows past ability.
The past of 'can' is 'could'.
Answer: could
quiz.mistake: Uses present 'can' for a past ability

quiz.q: Which word is closest in meaning to 'self-confidence'?
quiz.explain: Self-assurance means trust in one's own abilities.
steps: Self-confidence is trust in one's own abilities.
Its closest word is self-assurance; self-doubt and shyness are opposites.
Answer: self-assurance

teach.ask: Gappu: I'm scared to sing in front of the flock. Bholi was scared too. What helped her, and how do I say 'I am able to'?
teach.praise: La-la-chirp! With encouragement and practice, I CAN sing. Bholi did it, and so can I!
teach.nudge: What helped Bholi become confident? Which modal shows that you are able to do something?

revise.summary: Bholi stammered and was mocked as a child, but at school she learns to speak and read, and at the end she speaks firmly and decides to teach there. We also learn modals of ability, permission, obligation, advice and no necessity.
focus: Recall Bholi's difficulty and her decision at the end.
Choose the right modal for ability, permission, obligation, advice or no necessity.
Know the difference between 'must' and 'have to'.
remember: Ability (can, could), permission (may, can), obligation (must, have to), advice (should), no necessity (needn't).
'Must' shows strong obligation, often from the speaker; 'have to' often shows a rule from outside.
'Could' is the past of 'can' for ability: 'At five, I could swim.'
traps: Don't use 'must' for every instruction; 'needn't' shows no necessity.
Don't use present 'can' for a past ability; use 'could'.
